newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian privatisation minister Kokh quits.
newsitem.headline: Russian privatisation minister Kokh quits.

text.p: Russian privatisation minister Alfred Kokh has resigned and will be replaced by another ally of economic policy chief Anatoly Chubais.

A spokesman for President Boris Yeltsin said on Wednesday that Kokh, who resigned as Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the State Property Committee, would be replaced in both posts by Maxim Boiko, currently deputy head of Yeltsin's administration.
Previously Boiko headed the Russian Privatisation Centre.
Both Kokh and Boiko are close to Chubais, who is one of two first deputy prime ministers and the main architect of market reforms in Yeltsin's government.
A Kremlin source described Boiko as "a soldier of Chubais' party" who had long wanted to work more closely with his mentor.
Kokh, a stocky 36-year-old known for his acerbic manner, said he planned to set up his own company but did not disclose what kind of business it would be.
"He has long wanted to quit government service...He is a high-class professional in the legal, financial and economic fields," his secretary Victoria Vergelskaya told Reuters.
She said his resignation was not linked to political controversy surrounding Russia's latest spate of state sell-offs.
Kokh has presided over a particularly stormy phase of Russian privatisation and was singled out for criticism recently by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
The biggest sell-off yet, the sale last month of one quarter of telecoms company Svyazinvest, prompted an unprecedented outcry in media controlled by businessmen linked to the losing consortium.

The sale this month of a controlling 38 percent stake in Russia's biggest mining company Norilsk Nickel, also proved controversial, with Chernomyrdin unsuccessfully trying to have the sale stopped at the last minute.

Kokh also halted the controversial privatisation of Russia's biggest insurer, Rosgosstrakh, in June. Company management, which stood to win a large stake in the insurer, is suing the State Property Committee over the suspension.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, Kokh said he had tried to quit government service as early as 1995 but had been told that "first he must launch the process of cash privatisation and make it work smoothly".
Recent sales, including Svyazinvest which netted $1.88 billion for state coffers, showed the country was now able to profit handsomely from privatisation.
"Now I can go into the private sector with a quiet conscience," Kokh said.
The Kremlin press service said Yeltsin was satisfied with Kokh's performance and had thanked him for his work in "one of the most difficult spheres of government".
Yeltsin also praised Boiko for his previous work in the presidential administration.
Kremlin sources said Wednesday's changes had very limited political significance though they could entail some loss of influence for Chubais in the presidential administration.
Chubais is widely seen as a kingmaker in the next presidential election, due in 2000.
The Kremlin sources said Boiko would provide "a tough test for the State Property Committee" due to his reputation as a high-powered administrator.
The slim, bespectacled intellectual wrote a book in 1995 called "Privatising Russia".
